extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary and historical criticism; historians, translators, and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging political treatises, historical works, translations, and literary style — focusing on accuracy, fairness, style, applicability, and the trade‑off between vividness and fidelity. Useful for critics, students, and translators assessing 19th‑century or classical political/historical texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of subject details
rubrics_metrics.description: "He made himself master of all its details."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author should study the technical theory and practical details of their subject with intense assiduity; intimate knowledge of particulars is a mark of competence and supports practical reform proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public exertions as moral/political credit
rubrics_metrics.description: "The exertions which he made to effect this great object ought alone to rescue his name from obloquy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author's real‑world efforts or public services (e.g., attempting institutional reform) can redeem reputation; evaluate figures not only on doctrine but on active attempts to improve affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity, grace, and animation of style
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ingenuity, the grace, and the perspicuity of the style, and the eloquence and animation of particular passages... must give pleasure even to readers who take no interest in the subject."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, graceful, ingenious, and animated prose is valuable in itself and can engage readers outside the specialist audience; style can confer broad appeal regardless of subject interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value as commentary on contemporary history
rubrics_metrics.description: "As a commentary on the history of his times, it is invaluable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work illuminates its historical moment; a good political treatise or historical work should shed light on contemporary events and conditions, making it invaluable even to non‑specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral tone and ethical blemishes
rubrics_metrics.description: "On the peculiar immorality which has rendered The Prince unpopular... we cannot, however, deny that it is a great blemish."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral tenor of arguments and recommendations affects reception and merit; ethical faults diminish pleasure and should be weighed when judging a work's overall value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper balance of means and ends
rubrics_metrics.description: "In his political scheme, the means had been more deeply considered than the ends. The great principle... is not recognised with sufficient clearness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political theory should state and defend its ends (e.g., public happiness) as clearly as it develops means; neglecting ultimate purposes is a substantive defect in political writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and impartiality of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nothing is more remarkable in the political treatises of Machiavelli than the fairness of mind which they indicate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness — candidly acknowledging opposing views and admitting error where applicable — is a key virtue in political and historical writing and enhances credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual honesty; avoidance of sophistry
rubrics_metrics.description: "He never advances a false opinion because it is new or splendid... His errors are at once explained by a reference to the circumstances in which he was placed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid advancing positions for novelty or rhetorical effect; honest account of limits and context is preferable to dazzling but unsound theorising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of thought and diction; avoid obscurity and affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Propriety of thought, and propriety of diction, are commonly found together. Obscurity and affectation are the two greatest faults of style."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity of idea and clarity of expression go together; obscurity often signals confused thinking, and affectation (seeking to dazzle) corrupts both style and argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity often stems from confused ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: "Obscurity of expression generally springs from confusion of ideas; and the same wish to dazzle at any cost which produces affectation... is likely to produce sophistry in his reasonings."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating prose, probe whether opaque phrasing masks unclear thought or deliberate rhetorical manoeuvre; prefer lucidity rooted in sound ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stylistic tricks that conceal weak reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every trick of expression... is employed to disguise the fallacy of some positions, and the triteness of others. Absurdities are brightened into epigrams; truisms are darkened into enigmas."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be critical of authors who use epigrams, paradoxes, or obscure phrasing to mask weak or trivial content; style should reveal, not conceal, argumentative strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnestness and emotional engagement enhance interest
rubrics_metrics.description: "The political works of Machiavelli derive a peculiar interest from the mournful earnestness which he manifests whenever he touches on topics connected with the calamities of his native land."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincere emotional engagement with subjects of suffering or national calamity can increase a work's interest and moral weight — judged positively when not excessive or merely rhetorical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone appropriateness; avoid corrosive bitterness or levity
rubrics_metrics.description: "His enthusiasm... seems to have found a vent in desperate levity... The sarcastic bitterness of his conversation disgusted those..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tone for decorum and suitability: bitterness, vindictiveness, or frivolous levity can undermine the author's dignity and alienate readers; moderation is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical fidelity and research diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: "The History does not appear to be the fruit of much industry or research. It is unquestionably inaccurate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy, documentary research, and industry are central to the merits of historical writing; lack of thorough research is a serious flaw even if prose is appealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative vividness and picturesque effect vs strict accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is elegant, lively, and picturesque... The best portraits are perhaps those in which there is a slight mixture of caricature... The relation is, no doubt, in all its principal points, strictly true. But the numerous little incidents... are evidently furnished by the imagination of the author."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a recognised trade‑off: a certain judicious exaggeration or imaginative reconstruction can heighten effect and impart vivid impressions, but historians should not misrepresent principal facts; clearly signal imaginative additions when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable embellishment for effect must be judged against truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "Something is lost in accuracy; but much is gained in effect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When embellishment improves reader understanding or memorability, it may be defensible — but critics should weigh gains in effect against losses in factual accuracy and be explicit about departures from strict documentary truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation quality: skill, taste, and scrupulous integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Of the translation we need only say that it is such as might be expected from the skill, the taste, and the scrupulous integrity of the accomplished lady..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess translations for fidelity to original meaning, stylistic judgment, cultural mediation (translator as interpreter between minds), and scrupulous integrity rather than mere literalness or flashy language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects of enduring significance and illuminate central questions
rubrics_metrics.description: "How it was that Protestantism did so much, yet did no more... is certainly a most curious and important question; and on this question Professor Ranke has thrown far more light than any other person who has written on it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work's importance is increased when it addresses central, long‑standing questions and sheds new light; subject selection and ability to illuminate matter for judging scholarly value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate theological propositions from empirical/physical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: "The books and traditions of a sect may contain... other propositions... which relate to physics. If new discoveries should throw discredit on the physical propositions, the theological propositions... will share in that discredit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors dealing with religion should distinguish theological claims from empirical assertions; failure to separate them risks undermining theological claims when empirical parts are disproved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of disciplinary limits: some fields are non‑progressive
rubrics_metrics.description: "Natural theology, then, is not a progressive science."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating works in theology or metaphysics, recognise that methods and evidentiary bases differ from experimental or mathematical sciences; do not assume the same model of cumulative progress applies.
